candidates.source_title: Rochdale council steps up regeneration drive in deal for landmark site - TheBusinessDesk.com
candidates.source_body_excerpt: Rochdale Borough Council has struck a deal to acquire Middleton’s Warwick Mill, in a boost to the ongoing regeneration of the area. Built in 1907, the Grade II-listed structure stopped operating as a cotton mill in 1965 and has been vacant for at least a decade. In recent years, alongside its neighbour, 1960’s office building, London House, which the council is also hoping to acquire under the terms of the deal, the site has become an eyesore and a target for vandalism. For the past decade the council has been working with the private sector to find a solution for the imposing structure but none of the plans came to fruition and its condition has been gradually deteriorating. The council has been looking at buying the mill for a period of time, but a recent engagement exercise with local residents and businesses galvanised its decision. The exercise – ‘Our Town, Our Future’ – saw local community organisation, Middleton Co-operating, engage with more than 2,000 residents to find out what they wanted for the area as part of wider work to create a Mayoral Development Corporation (MDC) for the area, which will be chaired by Middleton-born actor and comedian, Steve Coogan, and Rose Marley, chief executive of Co-operatives UK. Around a third of respondents said they would like to see Warwick Mill brought back into use. A number of people responding to the survey said that the building has huge potential and should be sensitively restored and brought back into use for the benefit of the wider community. Cllr Neil Emmott, leader of Rochdale Borough Council, said: “Warwick Mill is an important landmark in Middleton and serves as a striking visual reminder of the area’s rich history as a major player in the global cotton trade.

candidates.source_title: Rochdale council agrees deal to buy Middleton's Warwick Mill - Roch Valley Radio
candidates.source_body_excerpt:
The council is also hoping to acquire neighbouring London House under the terms of the deal.

Warwick Mill was built in 1907 and stopped operating as a cotton mill in 1965. The council said it has been vacant for at least a decade and its condition has deteriorated.

The council has worked with the private sector over the past decade to find a new use for the building, but previous plans did not go ahead.

Its decision to pursue the purchase follows the Our Town, Our Future engagement exercise carried out by community organisation Middleton Co-operating.

More than 2,000 residents took part, with around a third saying they wanted to see Warwick Mill brought back into use.

The engagement forms part of wider work to establish a Mayoral Development Corporation for Middleton, which will be co-chaired by Middleton-born actor and comedian Steve Coogan and Co-operatives UK chief executive Rose Marley.

Councillor Neil Emmott, leader of Rochdale Borough Council, said: “Warwick Mill is an important landmark in Middleton and serves as a striking visual reminder of the area’s rich history as a major player in the global cotton trade. It also represents a huge regeneration opportunity and a chance to really revitalise this key part of the town centre.

“Middleton’s MDC will be based on cooperative values, with the community, businesses, voluntary sector, council and GMCA all working together to bring about positive changes. The desire to bring Warwick Mill back into use came through very clearly in the engagement exercise and we’ve responded to this.”

The acquisition was announced at an event at Middleton Arena which provided an update on the consultation and formation of the development corporation.

Steve Coogan, Rose Marley, Greater Manchester mayor Bev Craig and Councillor Emmott attended the event.

Marley said: “More than 2,000 people gave their time to Our Town, Our Future – the biggest conversation Middleton has ever had about its own future. What came back was clear: people want to see regeneration done with Middleton, not to Middleton.

“The Middleton Co-operative Mayoral Development Corporation will help to carry that mandate forward: into the town's housing, transport, green spaces and public buildings – Warwick Mill among them – and into every decision still to be made.”

A feasibility study is under way to consider possible future uses for Warwick Mill, with the council saying the community will be consulted on the final plans.

The council plans to carry out urgent repairs, improve security and tidy the land around the building within the next few months.

candidates.source_title: Warwick Mill: Council is in control and pledges to move it forward - Rochdale Times
candidates.source_body_excerpt: Contractors are securing Warwick Mill and weighing up the options as Rochdale Council completes its purchase of the historic mill in Middleton. The council announced yesterday that it is in the process of buying the Grade II-listed building and neighbouring London House from Chinese developer Kam Lei Fong and is starting essential work to make the building safe and secure. The price of the purchase has not been disclosed because it is commercially sensitive but the sale is expected to be completed in the next few weeks. Following the announcement, council leader Cllr Neil Emmott explained the reason for buying the site. He said: “A big bugbear for the people of Middleton for many years, has been Warwick Mill. “It is a fantastic listed building but has, unfortunately, gone to rack and ruin and has become something of an eyesore in our town centre when it could be something far better and it attracts antisocial behaviour. “For a number of years now, we’ve been trying to negotiate with different owners, because the ownership of the mill has changed a couple of times. With the mill deteriorating further, town hall bosses have made the decision to buy the land in order to push through redevelopment. candidates.source_title: ‘Success regenerating Middleton isn’t a £6 oat milk latte’ - Rochdale Times
candidates.source_body_excerpt: The pride residents feel in Middleton and their desire for real change could help drive improvements across Greater Manchester, according to the region’s mayor. Bev Craig was one of the panellists at last night’s Our Town, Our Future event at Middleton Arena, where organisers Middleton Co-operating shared feedback from a survey asking people what they want to see in Middleton and the proposed Mayoral Development Corporation. And, just hours after Rochdale Council announced it had purchased the historic site, bringing Warwick Mill back to life was top of the list many respondents, followed by making use of other empty buildings in the town. Many also called for the return of banking and Post Office services to the town centre, with a Post Office representative pledging a town centre office will return and is likely to open in the new year. The findings were delivered by host Kallum Nolan, of Middleton Co-operating, with a panel including MDC co-chairs Rose Marley and Steve Coogan welcoming guests on to the stage to discuss specific aspects of the findings and the way forward. “We’re dead proud of Midd” was the message that came through loud and clear as Ms Craig gave the MDC plans her full support, adding that success in Middleton could be a blueprint for the rest of the region. Rose Marley, Steve Coogan and Greater Manchester Mayor Bev Craig The mayor said: “I’ve spent a lot of time talking to people in Middleton already, and I think the thing that comes through is just high pride people have being from Middleton.

candidates.source_title: East Lancashire Railway welcomes its first female steam locomotive driver
candidates.source_body_excerpt:
She progressed through the railway's steam department from cleaner to fireman before qualifying to drive steam locomotives.

Steph is now officially a Passed Fireman, allowing her to carry out both firing and driving turns on the heritage railway.

She said her interest in heritage railways began when she attended her first Santa Special at two months old.

Steph said: “I’m so pleased to be able to say that I’ve now successfully passed all my driving assessments to become the first female steam train driver at the East Lancashire Railway. It feels like such a huge achievement, and I still can’t quite believe that I’m now officially a Passed Fireman, allowing me to carry out both firing and driving turns.

“My love of heritage railways goes back to when I was just two months old, when I attended my first Santa Special. To think that, all these years later, I would be here achieving this is something I could never have imagined. From being a little girl fascinated by steam trains to now having the opportunity to drive one myself is a dream come true.

“I’m incredibly grateful to everyone who has supported, encouraged and helped me along the way. There have been challenges and a lot to learn, but every step of the journey has made reaching this moment even more rewarding.

“I hope my achievement will show other women that the railway really is a place for them. If my journey inspires even one woman to take that first step, get involved and discover what they can achieve, then I would be incredibly proud.”

Mike Kelly, chairman of the East Lancashire Railway, said: “I want to offer Steph my warmest congratulations on this outstanding achievement. Becoming a steam locomotive driver requires enormous commitment, determination, skill and passion, and Steph has demonstrated all of those qualities throughout her journey.

“What makes this achievement particularly special is that Steph has become the first female steam locomotive driver in the history of the East Lancashire Railway.

“She may not see herself as a pioneer or a role model, but she should take a moment to appreciate what she has achieved. By following the traditional route from cleaner through the steam crew ranks to the footplate, she has not only achieved her own ambition but has also helped to open the door for other women who may dream of becoming steam locomotive drivers.”

The East Lancashire Railway operates around 12 miles between Heywood, Bury, Ramsbottom and Rawtenstall.

It reopened to passengers in 1987 and is due to celebrate its 40th anniversary in 2027.

A planning officer’s report states: “The property is vacant, having last been used as a nursing home for elderly people approximately 10 years ago. “The development would provide approximately 123 square metres of accommodation within the basement, approximately 229 square metres at ground floor level and approximately 200 square metres at first floor level, resulting in a total floorspace of approximately 552 square metres. “The proposed jewellery shop would occupy part of the ground floor, with the principal customer-facing retail sales area measuring approximately 137 square metres. The remaining accommodation would comprise ancillary storage, staff and operational areas associated with the proposed retail use. The basement and first floor would be utilised primarily for storage purposes.” In planning documents submitted with the application, a sequential assessment was carried out to compare alternative sites across the borough. It concluded that shopping centres which offered the desired floor space were too expensive for small businesses, and there were no suitable alternative premises available.

Three minutes later Lamin Sillah effectively wrapped up the three points. Eli King’s delivery was nodded down by Andy Smith and Sillah headed home. Dale were reduced to 10 men when Ed Francis saw red for a second bookable offence on the hour mark. Gills stopper Oliver Wright made a fine double save to deny Mani Dieseruvwe and Luke Hannant before Brophy scored a superb fourth. Midway through the second half Brophy drifted in from the left and dribbled the ball round four defenders before beating Ramming from close range. Dale debutant Charlie Tasker headed an 87th minute reply for the home side.
